title: The Impact of Gender Stereotypes on the Self-Concept of Female Students in STEM Subjects with an Under-Representation of Females
extended_summary:
This paper examines how gender stereotypes, school experiences, and family support relate to female students’ academic self-concept in STEM fields. The authors focus on a specific group that is often underrepresented in STEM: women studying STEM subjects with 30% or fewer female students, which they label STEM-LPF. The central research question asks whether women’s own stereotypes, compared with school- and family-related factors, predict how positively they evaluate their STEM abilities.

The main empirical component is a survey of 296 female university students from German universities enrolled in STEM-LPF subjects such as mechanical engineering, computer science, physics, metal engineering, civil engineering, and electrical engineering. Students reported their STEM self-concept, internalized gender stereotypes, school-related experiences such as favorite subjects and perceived teacher behavior, and family support in mathematics and STEM. The study also includes a small qualitative interview study with 11 female STEM students to illustrate the quantitative findings.

Results from the latent regression model show that stronger gender stereotypes are associated with lower STEM self-concept. School factors are mixed: having STEM as favorite school subjects relates positively to self-concept, while perceived school support and stereotyped teacher behavior relate negatively. Family support also shows a negative relationship with STEM self-concept, which the authors interpret as potentially intrusive or stereotype-reinforcing support rather than purely helpful assistance. Overall, the paper argues that stereotypes remain influential even among women who have already chosen gender-atypical STEM pathways, and that indirect, stereotype-sensitive forms of support may be more beneficial than direct intervention.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed correlational/latent regression study with a qualitative supplement, not an experimental test of an intervention. It provides useful evidence about associations among stereotypes, support, and self-concept, but cannot establish causal effects.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful associations for a priority population (female STEM students), including a moderate negative relation between stereotypes and STEM self-concept (β=-0.405). However, because it is observational and focuses on self-concept rather than direct achievement gains, the impact is indirect and not clearly generalizable as an intervention effect.

finding.finding_summary: This correlational latent regression study of female STEM-LPF university students (n=296) found that higher internalized gender stereotypes were associated with lower STEM academic self-concept (β=-0.405). The paper also found that school favorite STEM subjects predicted higher self-concept, while school support/teacher stereotypes and family support variables were negatively related to self-concept, explaining 30.4% of the variance in STEM self-concept overall (R²=0.304).
finding.measure: STEM academic self-concept; internalized gender stereotypes; school support/teacher stereotypes; family support
